design_detail: Swedish record-linkage comparison of drug-related deaths (DRDs) in five datasets, matched death by death on the personal identification number. Three come from the national mortality register (NMR), which is built from the mandatory death certificate: NMR/Sweden (a Swedish specification: any listed drug-related ICD code anywhere on the certificate, underlying or contributory cause; 1994–2012, N = 7,497), its Stockholm-area subset NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996, N = 1,181), and NMR/EMCDDA (the European specification: a listed code as the underlying cause only, from a shorter list; 1997–2012, N = 3,908). The fourth, Toxreg, is built from forensic toxicology alone: deaths in which an illegal drug, or methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause; ages 10–60, or any age if morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine were both found (1994–2012; N = 6,648 in Table I, 6,448 in the text and Figure 2). The reference standard is an inventory of DRDs in the Stockholm area in 1985–1996 (1,061 forensic cases and 151 hospital cases, N = 1,212), each death assessed individually. NMR/Stockholm (12 years) and Toxreg (1994–1996 only) were matched to the inventory, and NMR deaths missing from it were classified by the authors from the certificate. For 1994–2012 the national datasets were compared only with each other (overlap, size, age, sex, annual counts and, by Toxreg's main drug, capture by NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA), without a reference standard.
can_establish: How far, in the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, a certificate-based ICD-code selection and (for 1994–1996) a forensic-toxicology register agreed death by death with an inventory of individually assessed drug-related deaths, in both directions (inventory deaths missing from each source, and deaths in each source that the inventory did not count), and how much three Swedish national selections overlapped and differed in size, age, sex and main drug in 1994–2012.
cannot_establish: How accurate Swedish certificate-based or toxicology-based counts were after 1996 (nothing later was compared with a reference), how accurate the EMCDDA selection is (it was never compared with the inventory), whether the drugs counted in Toxreg caused the deaths (Toxreg counts presence), or anything about other countries; and because the reference inventory counted deaths of people with a personal history of drug use as drug-related whatever the cause, as the paper describes it, the deaths 'missed' by the registers are not all missed drug poisonings.

sample.recruitment: Registers and an inventory; no recruitment. NMR: the causes of death on death certificates, which Swedish law makes mandatory for all deaths, entered into the national mortality register kept by the National Board of Health and Welfare, with attrition of about 1% (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). Toxreg: forensic toxicology results in the registers of the National Board of Forensic Medicine (pp. 3, 7). Inventory: begun as an attempt to estimate the true number of HIV-related deaths in the Stockholm area, first including all known cases of 'lethal injection' and then expanded to all decedents with a personal history of drug use problems (the paper's term is drug abuse) or with illegal drugs present at death; its main sources were examination records of the Stockholm forensic institute and medical records of HIV-related hospital deaths (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: NMR/Sweden and NMR/Stockholm: any code in Table II anywhere on the certificate (ICD-9 for 1994–1996: 292, 304.0–304.9, 305.2–305.3, 305.5–305.7, 305.9, 965.0, 968.5, 969.6, 969.7; ICD-10 from 1997: F11–F16, F18, F19, O35.5, P04.4, T40.0–T40.9, T43.6, Z50.3, Z71.5, Z72.2). NMR/EMCDDA: underlying cause only and a shorter list, without F13, F18, O35.5, P04.4, T40.4 or the Z codes (Table II, p. 4). Table II lists no external-cause codes, and the paper does not say how intent was handled. Toxreg: an illegal drug or methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl found at forensic toxicology, ages 10–60 (any age with morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine), whatever the certified cause (p. 3). Inventory: deaths involving illegal drugs or non-prescribed morphine or methadone, and deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems; deaths involving prescribed methadone or morphine, including suicide with morphine prescribed for pain, were not counted (p. 3).
sample.demographics: 1997–2012: NMR/Sweden mean age 43 years, 24.4% women; NMR/EMCDDA mean age 40, 16.1% women; Toxreg mean age 37, 16.5% women (p. 5). No demographics are given for the Stockholm inventory or for the deaths each source missed.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registers). NMR attrition about 1% (p. 2); the cause-of-death register covers more than 99% of deaths and the forensic database more than 90% of non-natural deaths below age 65 (p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: The validation rests on one region in 1985–1996, when many deaths of people who used drugs were HIV-related; the authors note fewer HIV deaths, more hepatitis C, older ages, more chronic drug-related organ damage and more prescription-opioid use today (p. 7). Toxreg could be validated only for 1994–1996, cannot capture deaths that were not forensically examined (the hospital cases, 151 in the whole 1985–1996 inventory; how many fell in 1994–1996 is not given) and excludes ages over 60 unless morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine were both found. The periods compared differ: NMR/Stockholm against 12 years of the inventory, Toxreg against 3. Stockholm residents who died elsewhere were outside the inventory's reach (21 of the 30 drug-related NMR deaths it missed).

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. NMR: a physician completes the mandatory death certificate; the National Board of Health and Welfare registers it, and the causes are ICD-coded by the statistical office (pp. 2, 7–8). A death enters NMR/Sweden if any listed code appears anywhere on the certificate, and NMR/EMCDDA only if the underlying cause is a listed code (pp. 2–3; Table II). Toxreg: forensic toxicology alone, the presence of an illegal drug or of methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, regardless of the certified cause (p. 3). Inventory: each death was assessed individually as due to drug use or not; who assessed is not stated, and the inventory's sources are described with reference to the first author's 1997 doctoral thesis (ref 20) (p. 3). NMR deaths absent from the inventory were classified by the authors from the causes on the certificate (pp. 3–4). What was tested: 1,061 of the 1,212 inventory deaths (87.5%, editors' calculation) were forensic cases, and 10% of these had a history of drug use but no positive toxicology (p. 5); the toxicology panel, specimens and the share of deaths tested outside the inventory are not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. 'Injection deaths' (accidents or suicides) are mentioned as a manner-of-death group without definition (p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Toxreg and the inventory count each death once, under a main drug chosen by a priority order based on relative toxicity in Nordic drug deaths: heroin or morphine, methadone, buprenorphine, fentanyl, amphetamine, cocaine, other drugs, THC (the inventory without buprenorphine and fentanyl, absent in 1985–1996); other drugs, pharmaceuticals and alcohol are recorded in Toxreg but not analysed (p. 3). The NMR selections count a death once if any listed code appears; the codes do not separate illegal from other drugs, and T40.4 covers drugs as different as buprenorphine, dextropropoxyphene, fentanyl, pethidine and tramadol (p. 7).

comparison.controls: Reference standard: the 1985–1996 Stockholm inventory, for NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996) and Toxreg (1994–1996). For 1997–2012 the national selections are compared only with each other, without a reference.
comparison.matching: Deaths linked one to one on the Swedish personal identification number (pp. 3–4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Why the certificate-based selection missed inventory deaths was not examined death by death, except for the hospital deaths; the inventory's own accuracy and the reliability of its individual assessments are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Share of inventory deaths found in each dataset; deaths in each dataset absent from the inventory, with reasons; values labelled sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value with 95% confidence intervals (p. 5); overlap counts (Figure 2), annual counts (Figure 1), mean age and share of women (p. 5), and the share of Toxreg deaths, by main drug, found in NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA (Table III).
outcomes.validity_norms: The reference inventory is not validated, and its definition of a drug-related death is broader than either register specification: deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems counted whatever the stated cause (p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Captured = the inventory death appears in the dataset under its ICD-code or toxicology rule. Not drug-related = a dataset death absent from the inventory, unless the authors judged it drug-related from its certificate (pp. 3–4). The paper labels as sensitivity the share of each dataset's deaths that were in the inventory, and as positive predictive value the share of inventory deaths found in the dataset: the reverse of the usual definitions with the inventory as the reference (reporting issue 1).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions with confidence intervals; trends compared by eye (Figure 1), without statistics.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The authors classified the unmatched NMR deaths themselves; the reference inventory is described with the first author's doctoral thesis (ref 20) and Toxreg's method was developed in connection with it (ref 18).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive. Stockholm 1985–1996: 761 of 1,212 inventory deaths in NMR/Stockholm (62.8%), 451 not (37.2%, editors' calculation); 734 of 1,061 forensic cases (69%), from 80% (heroin) to 13% (cocaine) by main drug; 81% of 'injection deaths'; 28% of 151 hospital deaths (as printed). NMR/Stockholm held 419 deaths absent from the inventory, 30 of them judged drug-related, so 389 of its 1,181 deaths (33%) were not drug-related by the inventory (editors' calculation). Printed statistics: 'sensitivity' 64.5% (95% CI 61.7–67.2), specificity 99.9 (99.90–99.92), 'PPV' 62.8 (60.4–65.1). Toxreg 1994–1996: 317 of 454 inventory deaths (69.8%), 137 not (30.2%, editors' calculation); 43 Toxreg cases not inventory deaths (medical treatment); printed 'sensitivity' 88.1% (95% CI 84.3–81.2), specificity 99.7 (99.6–99.8), 'PPV' 69.8 (66.1–73.3). National 1994–2012: 4,238 deaths in both NMR/Sweden and Toxreg, 2,210 in Toxreg only (34%), 3,259 in NMR/Sweden only (43%); NMR/EMCDDA and Toxreg shared 2,840 (editors' calculation), with 3,608 in Toxreg only and 1,068 in NMR/EMCDDA only. Table III capture of Toxreg deaths by main drug, NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA: heroin 96% and 90%, THC 23% and 9%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The study is covered by an approval of the Stockholm Regional Ethics Review Board (p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Several breakdowns are 'data not shown': capture by manner of death, the 49 non-drug deaths, the hospital deaths and Toxreg's missed hospital cases (p. 5). The reasons for about 333 of the 389 NMR/Stockholm deaths judged not drug-related are not given (editors' calculation: 419 − 30 − 49 − 7). No NMR figure for 1994–1996 alone is reported, which would have allowed a like-for-like comparison with Toxreg. The denominators of the specificity values are not given.
analysis.power: Not applicable (complete registers and an exhaustive inventory).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In Stockholm in 1985–1996, a certificate-based selection held 761 of 1,212 deaths classed as drug-related by an individual-review inventory (63%) and 419 deaths the inventory did not hold, only 30 of which the authors judged drug-related; its total (1,181) was therefore close to the inventory's while about a third of the deaths differed in each direction. In 1994–1996 a toxicology-based register held 317 of 454 inventory deaths (70%), plus 43 deaths reflecting medical treatment. Nationally (1994–2012), certificate- and toxicology-based selections shared 4,238 of 9,707 deaths, differed in age and sex, and moved in the same direction year to year, at different levels.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title's 'miss one-third' is arithmetically supported (37% of inventory deaths not captured) but needs three qualifications the abstract does not give: the reference inventory counted deaths of people with a personal history of drug use as drug-related (p. 3), including 151 hospital deaths that were mainly HIV-related, so the missed deaths are not all missed drug poisonings; the same selection over-included about as many deaths, so its total was nearly right, as the Discussion concedes (p. 8); and the figures come from one region in 1985–1996. The Discussion's statement that one-third of certificates for inventory deaths 'did not mention drugs' (p. 7) is an inference, because the missed deaths' certificates were not examined. The Conclusions' 'statistics based on forensic toxicology were more complete' (p. 9) compares 3 years (Toxreg) with 12 (NMR), and the Results pair it with mislabelled statistics, including a Toxreg sensitivity of 88.1% that is in fact the share of Toxreg cases confirmed by the inventory. 'DRDs due to poisoning were captured well in all three datasets' (p. 9) has no figure behind it, and NMR/EMCDDA was never compared with the inventory. The conclusion that time trends were 'remarkably consistent' (p. 9) and can be compared between countries rests on visual inspection of Swedish series whose ratios changed over time; no other country was analysed.

timeline.event: Fugelstad, doctoral thesis on drug-related deaths in Stockholm 1985–1994 (ref 20), with which the paper describes the reference inventory's sources.

Eksborg and Rajs (Substance Use & Misuse; ref 18): causes and manners of death in relation to post-mortem tests for illegal drugs; the paper says Toxreg's method was developed in connection with the Stockholm inventory, citing this work.
EMCDDA standard protocol version 3.2 for the drug-related deaths key indicator (ref 10), the source of the European specification used for NMR/EMCDDA.

Amundsen (International Journal of Drug Policy): linkage of Norway's Cause of Death and Police Registries for 2007–2009, reporting lack of overlap between the two sources (by its listed title; read by another reader in this round).

Ruhm (card sc_ruhm_2018) and Buchanich et al. (card sc_buchanich_2018): US national corrections for overdose certificates naming no drug, a different source of undercounting, estimated by assumption rather than linkage.

Chen et al. (card sc_chen_2025): England and Wales, national counts naming specific opioids against projections from coroner-reported cases with toxicology, without linkage; undercounting only is examined.

replication.where_it_stands: The Stockholm validation has not been repeated; the authors describe it as still the only study of its type in the Stockholm area (p. 2). The US and English studies read for this round (cards sc_buchanich_2018, sc_horon_2018, sc_ruhm_2018, sc_chen_2025) estimate undercounting of specific drugs from a second source, a protocol or an assumption, not from an individually assessed inventory, and none measures over-inclusion. The 'one-third missed' applies to Stockholm in 1985–1996 and to an inventory that counted deaths of people with a history of drug use whatever the cause; in the same data the certificate-based total was close to right. It should not be carried to Sweden today, where the authors expect more chronic and older drug-related deaths (p. 7), or to other countries.

funding.funder: None: the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of the article (Funding, p. 9 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship or publication of the article (Declaration of conflicting interests, p. 9 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Karolinska Institute, Department of Clinical Neuroscience (Fugelstad, Ramstedt); Uppsala University, Section for Forensic Medicine (Thiblin) and Section for Social Medicine (Johansson). The reference inventory is described with the first author's 1997 doctoral thesis (ref 20), the 2016 report cited for Toxreg's coverage is by the first author (ref 14), and Toxreg's method was developed in connection with the inventory (ref 18), so the authors evaluate datasets partly built on their own earlier work; the fourth author's thesis concerns errors in death certificates (ref 6). Flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A new validation in a recent period: all deaths, or a random sample, in one or more regions (including people who died without forensic examination), each assessed by reviewers blind to the register outcome against written definitions that separate drug poisonings from other deaths of people who use drugs, then matched to the certificate-based (Swedish and EMCDDA) and toxicology-based selections, reporting both directions with correctly labelled sensitivity and positive predictive value; ideally repeated in a country with fewer forensic examinations.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Mandatory death certificates and the forensic registers are the right frames, but the validation covers one region in 1985–1996 (Toxreg only 1994–1996), while the headline is applied to national and international statistics of other periods.
An exhaustive inventory and complete register extracts, linked by personal identification number; no sampling.
1,212 inventory deaths (454 in 1994–1996) and 9,707 national deaths.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Datasets and the code lists from 1994 are described; the codes used for 1985–1993, the toxicology panel, who assessed the inventory deaths and how, and the inventory's demographics are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All linked records are counted, but the reasons for about 333 of the 389 certificate-selection deaths judged not drug-related, and for the missed inventory deaths other than hospital cases, are not examined; key breakdowns are 'data not shown'.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The reference inventory assessed each death individually, but it is not validated and its definition counts deaths of people with a personal history of drug use whatever the cause, so 'missed' mixes missed poisonings with deaths the register specifications were not designed to count; Toxreg counts presence, not cause.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Who assessed the inventory deaths, against which written criteria and with what agreement is not reported; the unmatched certificate deaths were classified by the authors, unblinded and without a second reader.

Sensitivity and positive predictive value are interchanged, one interval is impossible and two are narrower than their counts allow, several totals disagree between table, text and figure, the specificity denominators are not given, and trends are compared only by eye.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents; register attrition is about 1%.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a record-linkage study of death counts (round brief, certificate studies), although the study has the form of an accuracy comparison against a reference inventory. The death-by-death counts (761 of 1,212; 419 extra deaths, 30 of them drug-related; 317 of 454; 4,238 of 9,707 shared nationally) are direct and citable with their definitions. Overall risk of bias is high because the reference standard counts deaths of people with a history of drug use whatever the cause, the summary statistics readers would quote are mislabelled or internally inconsistent, and the validation is regional and 20–30 years old. Citable for: in Stockholm 1985–1996 the certificate-based selection captured about 63% of inventory deaths and also included about as many deaths the inventory did not count, so the totals were similar while the individual deaths differed; certificate-based and toxicology-based national counts shared under half of their combined deaths in 1994–2012 and differed in age, sex and main drug. Not citable for: the printed sensitivity of 88.1% as the toxicology register's capture; 'one-third' as the share of drug poisonings missed by current statistics; anything about other countries.

key_findings.finding: In the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, the certificate-based selection (NMR/Stockholm) contained 761 of the 1,212 deaths in the reference inventory (63%). The paper prints sensitivity 64.5% (95% CI 61.7–67.2), specificity 99.9 (95% CI 99.90–99.92) and positive predictive value 62.8 (95% CI 60.4–65.1). By editors' calculation, 451 inventory deaths (37%) were not in NMR/Stockholm.
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table I (p. 3) for the period
key_findings.note: The labels are interchanged (reporting issue 1): 761/1,212 = 62.8% is the share of inventory deaths captured, and 64.5% fits 761 of the 1,180 NMR/Stockholm deaths (761 matched plus 419 unmatched), the share of certificate-selected deaths that were in the inventory; its printed interval reproduces exactly (editors' calculation). The specificity denominator is not given.

key_findings.finding: Of the 1,061 forensically examined inventory deaths, 734 (69%) were in NMR/Stockholm; by main drug, capture was highest for heroin (80%) and lowest for cocaine (13%), and 81% of 'injection deaths' (accidents or suicides) were captured. Of the 151 hospital deaths in the inventory (described as mainly HIV-positive people who used drugs) only 28% were in NMR/Stockholm, the most important under-coverage (breakdowns: data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 761 captured overall minus 734 forensic cases leaves 27 hospital deaths (17.9% of 151), not 28% (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: In the other direction, NMR/Stockholm contained 419 deaths absent from the inventory. Judged by the authors from the causes on the certificates, only 30 were drug-related deaths: 21 Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and were not examined at the Stockholm forensic department, and 9 missed for administrative reasons such as forensic records lent or mislaid. Of the remainder, 49 were suicidal bathtub drownings after ingestion of various pharmaceuticals or deaths related to alcohol or pharmaceuticals rather than illegal drugs, and in 7 no cause of death had been found (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 389 of the 1,181 NMR/Stockholm deaths (33%) were not drug-related by the inventory, and the reasons for about 333 of them are not reported. The certificate-based total (1,181) was close to the inventory's (1,212) because over- and under-counting roughly offset.

key_findings.finding: In 1994–1996 Toxreg contained 317 of the 454 inventory drug-related deaths (70%). Of the Toxreg cases of those years, 43 were not inventory deaths because the forensic findings indicated medical treatment (in general opioid pharmaceuticals) rather than illicit use. The paper prints sensitivity 88.1% (95% CI 84.3–81.2), specificity 99.7 (95% CI 99.6–99.8) and positive predictive value 69.8 (95% CI 66.1–73.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: As for NMR/Stockholm the labels are interchanged, and one interval is impossible (reporting issues 1–4): 317/454 = 69.8% is the share of inventory deaths captured; 88.1% fits 317 of 360 Toxreg cases (317 + 43), the share of Toxreg cases confirmed by the inventory (editors' reconstruction; the paper writes 317, not 360, for the Toxreg cases). Cite 317 of 454 as Toxreg's capture, not 88.1%.

key_findings.finding: Toxreg cannot capture inventory deaths with a history of drug use but no positive toxicology, which made up 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases, nor hospital deaths that were not forensically examined; the paper says Toxreg did not capture 'the 151 hospital cases in the inventory' (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Period mismatch: the 1,061 forensic cases and the 151 hospital deaths belong to the whole 1985–1996 inventory, while Toxreg was compared only with the 454 inventory deaths of 1994–1996. How many hospital deaths, or toxicology-negative forensic cases, fall in 1994–1996 is not given, and Toxreg's 137 missed deaths (454 − 317) are not broken down (editors' reading).

key_findings.finding: National datasets: NMR/Sweden had 6,591 drug-related deaths in 1997–2012, mean age 43 years, 24.4% women; NMR/EMCDDA 3,908, mean age 40, 16.1% women; Toxreg 6,448, mean age 37, 16.5% women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 2 labels Toxreg's 6,448 as the 1994–2012 total (Table I gives 6,648), so the Toxreg figures may cover a longer period than the other two (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: NMR/Sweden and Toxreg, 1994–2012: 4,238 deaths were in both, 2,210 in Toxreg only (34% of Toxreg's 6,448) and 3,259 in NMR/Sweden only (43% of its 7,497); 9,707 deaths were in either.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: The counts are printed inside Figure 2, an image without a text layer (the text gives only the 34% and 43%); checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: NMR/EMCDDA and Toxreg: 3,608 Toxreg deaths were not in NMR/EMCDDA and 1,068 NMR/EMCDDA deaths were not in Toxreg; by editors' calculation 2,840 were in both (3,908 − 1,068 = 6,448 − 3,608).
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 3rd paragraph (continued on p. 6)
key_findings.note: 2,840 equals the sum of Table III's NMR/EMCDDA column (editors' sum). NMR/EMCDDA starts in 1997 while the 6,448 Toxreg deaths include 1994–1996 (Figure 2), so part of the 3,608 could never be in NMR/EMCDDA (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Share of Toxreg deaths, by Toxreg's main drug, also present in NMR/Sweden and in NMR/EMCDDA: heroin (819 deaths) 96% and 90%; morphine (1,495) 73% and 60%; methadone (688) 79% and 66%; buprenorphine (347) 76% and 66%; fentanyl (157) 72% and 70%; amphetamine (1,381) 56% and 22%; cocaine (122) 43% and 16%; other drugs (122) 36% and 18%; THC (700) 23% and 9%.
key_findings.locator: Table III; Results › Data description: General characteristics, 4th paragraph (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Period not stated; the Toxreg column sums to 5,831, which fits 1997–2012 (reporting issue 6). Because Toxreg counts presence, and includes deaths with cannabis as the only drug whatever the underlying cause (p. 8), a Toxreg death outside the NMR selections is not necessarily a missed drug poisoning. Fentanyl's 114 of 157 is 72.6% (printed 72).

key_findings.finding: Annual counts for 1997–2012 moved in the same direction in all three national datasets; NMR/Sweden and Toxreg were closer to each other than to NMR/EMCDDA, and at about the same level from 2006 apart from a Toxreg peak in 2008. No statistic compares the trends.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 prints no values. Approximate readings from a 300-dpi crop: NMR/EMCDDA about 150 (1997), 200 (2006) and 410 (2012); NMR/Sweden about 360, 330 and 520; Toxreg about 250, 300 and 525. NMR/Sweden was about 50 to 115 above Toxreg each year in 1997–2005, and NMR/EMCDDA rose from about two-fifths to about four-fifths of NMR/Sweden, so the series did not change in proportion. The approximate Toxreg readings for 1997–2012 sum to about 5,830, matching Table III's total.

key_findings.finding: The authors report that, in the comparison with the inventory, the NMR and toxicology datasets captured acute poisonings far better than chronic drug-related conditions, and expect recent data to cover total drug mortality less well because chronic conditions may now be more common; no figures are given beyond the heroin, cocaine, injection-death and hospital-death percentages.

The authors' summary in both directions: according to the inventory only two-thirds of the deaths in the NMR/Sweden dataset were related to drug use ('abuse-related'), yet the total numbers for Sweden are 'more or less correct'; NMR-based statistics would be a questionable basis for more detailed analyses.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Most useful statistics for international comparisons: numbers or trends?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The two-thirds comes from NMR/Stockholm in 1985–1996 and is applied here to NMR/Sweden.

key_findings.finding: Coverage of the sources: the cause-of-death register covers more than 99% of deaths and the forensic database more than 90% of non-natural deaths below age 65 in Sweden, including poisonings; attrition from the national mortality register is about 1%.
key_findings.locator: Datasets › Three NMR selections, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Discussion › Limitations and strengths, 2nd paragraph (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: ICD codes do not distinguish illegal from other drugs and some cover dissimilar substances: T40.4 (other synthetic narcotics) covers buprenorphine, dextropropoxyphene, fentanyl, pethidine and tramadol; the ICD specifications record neither other drugs present nor concentrations found at toxicology.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Toxreg requires only that a drug be found at forensic examination, so it includes deaths with cannabis as the only drug whatever the underlying cause (excluded by the EMCDDA specification) and some deaths in which a drug was present for reasons other than non-medical use, which the authors call few in their material; it misses drug-related deaths not due to acute intake, such as drug-related organ damage, and excludes ages over 60.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 3rd and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: In 1994–1996, 43 of about 360 Stockholm-area Toxreg cases (12%) reflected medical treatment (editors' reconstruction, key finding 4).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that basing international comparisons on numbers or rates of drug-related deaths gives misleading results, but that comparing trends is meaningful provided no major change in investigation or certification practice has occurred; no data from other countries were analysed.

The authors suggest that international comparisons of numbers of drug-related deaths based on mortality-register selections are made more problematic by varying forensic practices and by how fully official statistics cover deaths, especially of non-residents, and that this might at least partly explain why the Nordic and Baltic countries, with comparatively many forensic examinations, have higher rates of drug-related deaths than most other European countries. No other country's data were analysed; the suggestion rests on cited work (refs 8, 9) and is not tested here.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Most useful statistics for international comparisons: numbers or trends?, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In both validation paragraphs the value labelled positive predictive value is the share of inventory deaths found in the dataset (761/1,212 = 62.8%; 317/454 = 69.8%), which, with the inventory as the stated reference (p. 2; Table I), is the sensitivity; the value labelled sensitivity fits the share of the dataset's deaths that were in the inventory (761 of 1,180 = 64.5%, whose printed interval 61.7–67.2 reproduces exactly; 317 of 360 = 88.1%) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the counts. Capture of inventory deaths: 63% (certificate-based, 1985–1996) and 70% (Toxreg, 1994–1996); share of each dataset's deaths that were inventory deaths: about 64% (67% counting the 30 deaths the inventory missed) and 88%. The Discussion's statement that both sources included about the same amount of deaths not related to drug use (p. 7) matches the mislabelled values (62.8 and 69.8), not the counts (389 of 1,181 against 43 of about 360).

reporting_issues.issue: Toxreg's printed sensitivity of 88.1% has a 95% CI of 84.3–81.2: the upper limit lies below both the point estimate and the lower limit. For 317 of 360 a Wilson interval is 84.3–91.0 and an exact interval 84.2–91.2 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error, probably for about 91; the value is in any case the share of Toxreg cases confirmed by the inventory, not Toxreg's capture (issue 1).

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals printed for the values labelled positive predictive value are narrower than their counts allow: 60.4–65.1 for 761/1,212 (Wilson 60.0–65.5) and 66.1–73.3 for 317/454 (Wilson 65.4–73.9) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the uncertainty of the capture estimates is slightly larger than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text uses 317 for two different groups: the inventory deaths that Toxreg included (317 of 454) and the Toxreg cases of 1994–1996, of which 43 were not inventory deaths. Both cannot hold; the printed percentages fit 360 Toxreg cases (317 + 43, editors' reconstruction).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of Stockholm-area Toxreg cases in 1994–1996 is not printed; 360 is an inference from the percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Hospital deaths: 761 inventory deaths were captured overall and 734 of the 1,061 forensic cases, leaving 27 of the 151 hospital deaths (17.9%), but the text says 28% of the 151 (about 42) were in NMR/Stockholm (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the three figures is wrong and the breakdown is 'data not shown'; cite the overall 761 of 1,212.

reporting_issues.issue: Toxreg totals and periods disagree. Table I gives N = 6,648 for 1994–2012; the text and Figure 2 give 6,448, which Figure 2 labels 1994–2012 (4,238 + 2,210 = 6,448). The text sets this total beside 1997–2012 counts for NMR/Sweden (6,591) and NMR/EMCDDA (3,908), and the Methods say the age and sex description covers 1997–2012 (p. 4). Table III's Toxreg column sums to 5,831, and the 1997–2012 Toxreg line of Figure 1 to about the same (editors' sum and approximate reading), so Table III (period not stated) appears to cover 1997–2012, while the comparison with NMR/EMCDDA (3,608 Toxreg deaths not in it) appears to include 1994–1996 Toxreg deaths, which NMR/EMCDDA cannot contain.
reporting_issues.consequence: For 1997–2012 alone, about 2,991 of 5,831 Toxreg deaths (51%) were outside NMR/EMCDDA, rather than 3,608 of 6,448 (56%) (editors' calculation, assuming Table III covers 1997–2012). The mean age and share of women printed for Toxreg may cover a different period from the other two datasets.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I says NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996) is derived from NMR/Sweden, whose period it gives as 1994–2012, and Table II gives codes only from 1994 (ICD-9 for 1994–1996, ICD-10 from 1997), so the selection rules for 1985–1993, most of the validation period, are not printed. The Methods name NMR/Stockholm for the 1997–2012 description that the Results give for NMR/Sweden (p. 4), and the Conclusions refer to the NMR/Sweden dataset for 1985–1996, which is NMR/Stockholm. NMR/Stockholm's 761 matched and 419 unmatched deaths make 1,180, against 1,181 in Table I.
reporting_issues.consequence: The codes behind the headline comparison cannot be checked for 1985–1993, and the dataset names are used interchangeably; attach the validation figures to NMR/Stockholm, 1985–1996.

reporting_issues.issue: Table III's column headings read GMR/Sweden and GMR/Europe for NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA, its period is not stated, and fentanyl's 114 of 157 is printed as 72% (72.6%). Table II excludes T40.4, which the Discussion says covers buprenorphine and fentanyl, from the EMCDDA selection, yet Table III shows NMR/EMCDDA holding 66% of Toxreg's buprenorphine and 70% of its fentanyl deaths; the paper does not say through which codes these deaths entered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The European selection's code list may be incompletely printed; cite Table III's capture figures as printed, with these caveats.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says about one-quarter of the inventory cases were missing from the toxicology-based dataset; the counts give 137 of 454 (30%) for 1994–1996 (editors' calculation), and Toxreg could not capture the hospital deaths at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 317 of 454 captured (70%), not one-quarter missing, and not the 88.1% labelled sensitivity.

verification.source_read: Online-first PDF (SAGE, Scandinavian Journal of Public Health, pages 1–9, accepted 5 September 2017), all 9 pages; its pages differ from the version of record (48(1):29–37), so anchors cite the online-first page numbers. Tables I–III and Figures 1–2 checked on rendered pages (Figure 1 cropped at 300 dpi; its values are approximate readings); proportions and intervals recomputed by script; no supplement.

disagreements.first_pass: Toxreg cannot capture inventory deaths with a history of drug use but no positive toxicology, which made up 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases, nor the 151 hospital deaths, which were not forensically examined (data not shown).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 327 (second reader) (missed): the 151 hospital deaths and the 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases refer to the whole 1985–1996 inventory, but Toxreg was compared only with the 454 inventory deaths of 1994–1996; how many hospital deaths or toxicology-negative forensic cases fall in 1994–1996 is not given, and Toxreg's 137 missed deaths are never broken down. Key finding 4 and the claim text repeat '151' as if it applied to 1994–1996.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted (rendered PDF p. 5, Toxreg paragraph; Table I, PDF p. 3): the paper itself sets the whole inventory's 151 and 1,061 inside the 1994–1996 Toxreg paragraph. Finding reworded and a note added on the period.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 327 (second reader) (missed): period mismatch (see key_findings[4].finding).

disagreements.first_pass: The validation rests on one region in 1985–1996, when many deaths of people who used drugs were HIV-related; the authors note fewer HIV deaths, more hepatitis C, older ages, more chronic drug-related organ damage and more prescription-opioid use today (p. 7). Toxreg could be validated only for 1994–1996, cannot capture deaths that were not forensically examined (all 151 hospital cases) and excludes ages over 60. The periods compared differ: NMR/Stockholm against 12 years of the inventory, Toxreg against 3. Stockholm residents who died elsewhere were outside the inventory's reach (21 of the 30 drug-related NMR deaths it missed).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 327 (second reader) (missed): period mismatch for the 151 hospital deaths.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: the 151 now carries its period; the age exception for heroin markers (PDF p. 3) added for completeness.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 327 (second reader) (missed): the Discussion suggests that frequent forensic examination may partly explain why Nordic and Baltic countries have higher drug-death rates than most other European countries; untested; relevant to the cross-country wording in the claims.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted (rendered PDF p. 8, Discussion › Most useful statistics…, 2nd paragraph): added as key finding 16, labelled as an untested suggestion.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 327 (second reader): agree (JBI-prevalence, overall high).
disagreements.resolution: Readers agree on the overall judgment; card set to ai-checked.
